entries.title: Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia strikes bridge
entries.summary: As air raid sirens sounded in Kyiv, Chancellor Merz called on President Putin to end his "senseless war" and announced new measures to support Ukraine, including plans for joint Ukrainian-German drone production.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Germany's Merz visits Kyiv amid Russian strikes

Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026

As air raid sirens sounded in Kyiv, Chancellor Merz called on President Putin to end his "senseless war" and announced new measures to support Ukraine, including plans for joint Ukrainian-German drone production.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."

Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:

"We are ready for ​talks, we are ‌ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once ​again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."

Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from German business, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.

"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.

Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.

Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."

Focus on ramping up drone production

Merz pledged further military and energy assistance during his visit, with Zelenskyy announcing a German support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).

The package includes €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs ahead of winter.

Zelenskyy said the two countries had reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), covering defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine.

According to German government sources cited by Reuters and the DPA news agency, the planned cooperation includes the development and delivery of thousands of interceptor drones capable of countering the fast, jet-powered drones Russia increasingly deploys against Ukrainian infrastructure.

The plans also envisage expanding production of long-range weapons capable of striking targets more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.

Merz emphasized that the partnership would also benefit Germany, with companies from both countries developing technology to strengthen their security.

"German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger," he said.

Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit

The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.

"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."

In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."

Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.

"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.

But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.

"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"

Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'

Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.

His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.

"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."

Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.

In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller

entries.title: Trump names AI czar to head White House task force
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump has chosen members to lead a new AI task force to coordinate the administration's response to the rapidly evolving technology.
entries.content:
October 4, 2026

US President Donald Trump has chosen members to lead a new AI task force to coordinate the administration's response to the rapidly evolving technology.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday announced a White House task force to coordinate the administration's response to artificial intelligence (AI).

The group will be led by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael and director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor.

The task force, named the "Super Intelligence Force" or SI, in accordance with the term that the president prefers over AI.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies," Trump said in Truth Social post on Sunday.

Trump under pressure to regulate AI

Trump in September said he would create a new AI force to oversee the development of the fast-moving technology, but has so far opposed any strict regulation that codifies pillars of AI safety into law.

"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said in the September post where he announced he was going to choose an AI czar.

Leading up to the midterm elections in November, Trump has been under pressure to address concerns about AI risks. AI researchers and tech CEOs have sounded the alarm about the existential threat that the technology can pose.

Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei, for example, published an essay last month in which he called for a global slowdown in the race to develop AI. His call was met with agreement from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO  Elon Musk. 

Trump, AI CEOs sign safety pact

The US president hosted a White House lunch for nearly 20 tech titans at the end of September, where he said there was an agreement in the room that there should be "tremendous self-regulation" by tech companies.

The tech leaders signed onto a one-page document that relies on companies to voluntarily follow through on their safety commitments. But the accord is largely symbolic since it is not an official order.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Torrential rain and flooding leave 2 dead and 1 missing in Spain's Catalonia region
entries.summary: Authorities warned of extreme danger around Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents urged to stay indoors.
entries.content:
October 4, 2026

Authorities warned of extreme danger around Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents urged to stay indoors.

Two people were reported dead on Sunday, with at least one person missing, after torrential rain triggered flooding in Spain's northeastern Catalonia region.

Authorities have warned of an "extreme danger" in parts of Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents in some areas urged to stay indoors.

What do we know about the victims?

One person died when a wall collapsed at a campsite in Tordera, north of Barcelona, while another drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, Catalan firefighters said.

Emergency services were also searching for a missing person in Pineda de Mar, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) north of Barcelona.

Catalan regional leader Salvador Illa urged residents to exercise "the greatest caution" and follow instructions from emergency services.

How badly has Catalonia been hit?

More than 100 millimeters (3.9 inches) of rain fell overnight in numerous locations, according to Spain's AEMET weather agency.

Civil protection authorities sent alerts to people living near the Besos River warning of a risk of it bursting its banks. Residents were told to move to upper floors if flooding occurred.

Homes were flooded and vehicles submerged in towns near Barcelona, while local rail services were disrupted.

Emergency crews rescued people trapped in vehicles on flooded streets in Granollers and other communities.

Flights at Barcelona airport were also canceled or delayed, while shops closed early and sporting and cultural events were called off.

What is causing the extreme weather?

The storms are linked to a weather phenomenon known in Spain as a DANA, traditionally called a "gota fria," or "cold drop."

It occurs when cold air high in the atmosphere meets warm, moisture-laden air rising from the Mediterranean, producing intense thunderstorms.

Spain's geography can amplify the effect, as moist air from the Mediterranean is forced upwards by mountain ranges separating the coast from the country's elevated interior.

The latest flooding comes almost two years after catastrophic floods linked to a DANA killed 238 people in eastern Spain, mostly in Valencia, in October 2024.

A study published in 2026 found that human-caused climate change intensified the rainfall during that disaster.

The findings apply only to the 2024 Valencia floods, and a separate analysis would be needed to determine the influence of climate change on the latest flooding in Catalonia.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Voting in Brazil's 2026 presidential election has begun, with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right populist President Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. Polls show the first round of voting will likely lead to a runoff.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil votes in tight election between Lula and Bolsonaro

Published October 4, 2026last updated October 4, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right populist President Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. Polls show the first round of voting will likely lead to a runoff.

Voting began in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking a fourth non-consecutive term and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeking to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro.

Polls have predicted a tight race between the two leading candidates, with neither likely to win more than 50% of the vote to avoid a runoff that would take place on October 25.

Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

Lula vows to 'defeat the far-right'

The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."

Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.

Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.

"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.

Bolsonaro calls for 'change'

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.

He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."

"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."

Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.  The US president called the case a "witch hunt."

The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."

Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.

Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. 

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.

In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.

In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.

Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Japan: US Marine arrested in Okinawa on suspicion of murder
entries.summary: The Japanese government has lodged an official protest with Washington after a US Marine was arrested on suspicion of murdering a woman in Okinawa — where incidents involving US service personnel are not uncommon.
entries.content:
October 4, 2026

The Japanese government has lodged an official protest with Washington after a US Marine was arrested on suspicion of murdering a woman in Okinawa — where incidents involving US service personnel are not uncommon.

A United States Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, Japan, police said Sunday, prompting an official protest from the Japanese government.

The 20-year-old lance corporal is suspected of robbing and murdering a 39-year-old woman in a hotel in Naha, the capital of Japan's most southernmost prefecture.

Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported that CCTV footage showed a foreign man entering a hotel room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and who voluntarily accompanied them to a local police station where he was arrested.

The suspect reportedly denies the charges.

What have Japanese officials said?

"The occurrence of ​such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable," said Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ​in a statement as Tokyo registered an official protest with Washington.

"The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation," she continued, also calling for "stricter discipline among US military personnel" and "thorough measures" to prevent a recurrence.

According to the local Asahi Shimbum newspaper, the brother of the victim said: "We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter."

The US Marine Corps confirmed that a serviceman assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station at Futenma, Okinawa, was in Japanese custody.

"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the ⁠highest ​standards of behavior," it said in a statement.

The US Ambassador to Japan, George Glass, said he had spoken with Japan's Foreign Ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues."

How many US Marines are in Okinawa — and why?

The United States has around 54,000 military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, stationed in Japan. Most are based in Okinawa, which the US captured during the Second World War and held until 1972.

Located only 100 kilometers (60 miles) from Taiwan at the closest point, Okinawa is considered by both Tokyo and Washington to be key in deterring potential aggression from China in the region.

But the US presence regularly stirs resentment among local residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel, with crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run incidents and drunk-driving accidents.

"Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," said Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.

According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, around 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Okinawa since 1972. In 2024, that number hit 80, the highest in 20 years.

Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine to seven years in prison after finding him guilty of choking and attempting to rape a young woman.

In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
entries.summary: Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where voters are taking part in parliamentary, presidential and local elections.
entries.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina

Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid

October 4, 2026

Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where voters are taking part in parliamentary, presidential and local elections.

Polling began in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday, with around 3.4 million voters eligible to take part in the Balkan country's general election.

Citizens are electing officials across multiple tiers of government, including members of the multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

They will also choose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic slowdown, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and a long-drawn-out political gridlock, with the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that links them.

The election will see adversary ethnic parties, the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH, pitted against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.

Polls close at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results expected to be released late Sunday.

What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and the two semi-autonomous entities.

Both entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war which was triggered by the breakup of Yugoslavia.

Simmering ethnic tensions

Currently in Bosnia and Herzegovina's populace, around half are Muslim Bosniaks, while 31% are Orthodox Serb and 15% are Catholic Croat.

The country has been peaceful in recent years but its ethnonationalist parties have kept the divisions alive even as voters say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric and division.

Milorad Dodik not on the ballot but still dominant in Republika Srpska

In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remains the key figure despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

Dodik-backed Savo Minic is running for the Republika Srpska's presidency.

Dodik wants close ‌ties with Serbia and Russia. He has just returned from Moscow where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.

What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.

The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.

Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.

Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.

EU ambitions

Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.

But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India news: Police order probe amid sexual harassment allegations against officers at Delhi protest
entries.summary: Three women journalists say police officers sexually harassed them as they covered protests demanding the resignation of India's election chief. Meanwhile, LGBTQIA influencer Mad Sandhu was shot dead in Amritsar.
entries.content:
India

India: Police probe harassment allegations at Delhi protest

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 4, 2026

Three women journalists say police officers sexually harassed them as they covered protests demanding the resignation of India's election chief. Meanwhile, LGBTQIA influencer Mad Sandhu was shot dead in Amritsar.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police to investigate sexual harassment allegations against officers amid protests at Delhi's Jantar Mantar
  • Punjab-based LGBTQIA influencer Mad Sandhu shot dead in Amritsar
  • Cockroach Janta Party set for round two with march to Delhi on October 10 demanding election chief's resignation
  • India beat Pakistan in the Asian Games gold medal match in Japan
  • Indian men clinch hockey gold after women secure Olympics berth with their own gold

Here are the top headlines from India on Saturday, October 3, and Sunday, October 4, 2026:

This Delhi scientist is on a mission to hunt down the city's hottest spots. She's already found that over 75% of the city is heat-stressed. What can help?

Skip next section India wraps up Asian Games campaign with 85 medals

India wraps up Asian Games campaign with 85 medals

India ended its 2026 Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya with 85 medals – including 21 golds – and finished fourth in the medal table.

The haul also included 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, putting India ahead of Uzbekistan, which also won 21 golds but fewer silvers. China topped the standings with 169 golds, followed by Japan and South Korea.

The last day of the Games was critical for the country, with India collecting nine medals, five of them gold.

The hockey teams completed a rare double, with the women beating China 1-0 on Friday and the men defeating Malaysia 5-1 on Saturday. Both sides also secured qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

India also won both the men's and women's titles in cricket and kabaddi.

Golfer Pranavi Urs scripted history by becoming the first Indian woman to clinch an Asian Games gold medal in the sport.

Finally, archery and shooting were the biggest medal earners, with archery yielding five golds and shooting 15 medals in total. At 17 years of age, Kumkum Mohod was another breakout star for India, delivering a historic golden double in recurve on her Asian Games debut.

Despite many firsts, the total falls short of India's record haul at Hangzhou in 2023, where the contingent won more than 100 medals, including 28 golds.

Skip next section Punjab-based queer influencer gunned down in Amritsar

Punjab-based queer influencer gunned down in Amritsar

Madhusudan "Mad" Sandhu, a Punjabi makeup artist and LGBTQ social media influencer, was shot dead by two unidentified men on a motorcycle in Amritsar on Saturday evening, local media reported.

Sandhu was attacked around 6 p.m. local time on Loharka Road, outside a car wash center. Bystanders rushed him to a hospital, where he died.

With over 200,000 followers on Instagram, he was known for speaking openly about makeup artistry, gender issues and LGBTQ rights. He ran a popular beauty salon and beauty academies in Amritsar.

Police registered a case based on a statement from his family.

"We have leads and will solve the case soon," Prabhjot Singh Virk, the city's Deputy Commissioner of Police (Investigation), said, according to local media.

While no arrests or motive have been announced, a social media post appeared soon after the shooting, claiming responsibility and accusing the victim of "spoiling" Punjab. This rhetoric was something Sandhu had regularly faced in his public life after being open about his sexuality.

Authorities said the post claiming responsibility was being looked into as part of the probe, NDTV reported.

Skip next section PICTURES — This Indian island could disappear in 10 years

PICTURES — This Indian island could disappear in 10 years

Skip next section Police order probe amid sexual harassment allegations against officers at Delhi protest

Police order probe amid sexual harassment allegations against officers at Delhi protest

Delhi Police have begun an inquiry into complaints by three women journalists who say they were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering protests against India's chief election commissioner. 

In a statement on social media, police said the complaints were referred to the Crime Branch for a "fair and impartial enquiry."

The allegations emerged as police detained protesters near New Delhi's Jantar Mantar for a second day on Saturday, after over 700 people were detained on Friday. Demonstrators have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a mass voter-roll revision that has removed millions of names. The commission denies wrongdoing.

Kumar has not publicly commented.

In a video shared by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, one journalist alleged that an assistant commissioner of police groped her while she filmed the detention of student activist Neha Bora. Police have not publicly responded to the specific allegation. 

Journalists and protesters gathered outside the Parliament Street police station demanding a report be filed, local media reported.

The Press Club of India expressed "shock and dismay" at the treatment of journalists and urged swift action. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi asked Home Minister Amit Shah to respond, noting that Delhi Police fall under his ministry.

Several student groups have called for a march from India Gate to Jantar Mantar on Sunday at 3 p.m. local time.

Meanwhile, opposition parties plan to march on the Election Commission on Tuesday, and the CJP has called for a mass mobilization in Delhi on October 10.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

Hello again!

This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, back with more from India this weekend.

Police are investigating sexual harassment allegations against its officers after scores of protesters were detained for a second straight day near New Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

Meanwhile, in the northern city of Amritsar, queer social media influencer and makeup artist Madhusudan "Mad" Sandhu was shot dead. Local authorities said a probe has been launched into his death.

Plus, India has wrapped up its Asian Games 2026 campaign with 85 medals, finishing fourth with a last-day gold rush.

For this and more, follow our live blog.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

India offered a strong show on the last day of the Asian Games, but we aren't done with sports for the day. A FIFA international friendly match between India and Brazil is set to kick off in Kolkata later today.

As I sign off to watch that, we will now pause our coverage for the day. But we will be back tomorrow with more on the latest from India!

Skip next section Indian men join women's hockey team in securing 2028 Olympics berth

Indian men join women's hockey team in securing 2028 Olympics berth

India's men's hockey team beat Malaysia 5-1 in Saturday's final to retain the Asian Games title, marking the first time the team has won back-to-back golds at the Games.

This came a day after India's women's team delivered one of the standout results of the Games, edging defending champions China 1-0 in Friday's final to end a 44-year wait for gold.

Forward Lalremsiami Hmarzote's goal in the 10th minute, backed by goalkeeper Savita Punia saving a penalty stroke from China's Zhang Ying before halftime, helped secure the win.

The victory was India's first women's hockey gold at the Asian Games since 1982 and also secured the team a direct qualification spot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Skip next section Pakistan summons Indian envoy over border killing of 2 civilians

Pakistan summons Indian envoy over border killing of 2 civilians

Pakistan summoned India's charge d'affaires in Islamabad on Saturday to lodge a "strong protest" over the alleged killing of two Pakistani civilians by India's Border Security Force (BSF) near the border in the Kasur district of Pakistan's Punjab.

Pakistan's Foreign Office said two unarmed civilians were killed and a third injured when BSF personnel opened fire in the Bedian sector on Friday, calling it "unprovoked and lethal force."

While there was no immediate comment from New Delhi, Indian media reported a conflicting account, saying the men were suspected of trying to enter the country.

Pakistan rejected any characterization of the men as "infiltrators."

The incident comes against a tense backdrop of a historically fraught relationship between the neighbors. It occurred a day after Pakistan's military publicly disputed an earlier Indian claim regarding a separate incident in Indian-administered Kashmir.

Skip next section WATCH — India's bought brides: women traded as commodities?

WATCH — India's bought brides: women traded as commodities?

States in northern India continue to face an abysmal sex ratio at birth, leading to a shortage of women in places like Haryana.

This has led to thousands of women from poorer regions being brought to the state and sold as brides, giving rise to a lucrative human trafficking trade.

Watch to learn more:

Skip next section India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain Asian Games cricket gold

India beat Pakistan by 19 runs to retain Asian Games cricket gold

India successfully defended their Asian Games men's cricket gold medal, beating rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in Saturday's final in Nisshin, Japan.

After posting 211-6 backed by Abhishek Sharma's 61 off 20 balls and a late effort from Tilak Varma and Shivam Dube, India restricted Pakistan to 192-6 despite a big knock of 96 off 51 balls from Hasan Nawaz.

Nawaz fell four runs short of a century on the final ball of the innings, when he was caught by wicketkeeper Sanju Samson off Dube's bowling. It marked Pakistan's first-ever appearance in a men's Asian Games cricket final.

The event also marked one of the game's fiercest rivalries played out on an unlikely stage: a converted baseball field in suburban Nagoya, where Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan queued for hours to fill the 2,500-capacity venue.

"I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan," Pakistan supporter Umer Dar, a 26-year-old Nagoya resident, told AFP.

"Even if it's in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there," added Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan. "Anywhere they play in the world, it's always crazy."

While cricket remains a niche sport in Japan, there has been growing local interest, as shown by India's first-ever T20 international against Japan last week, which India won by just two runs in a rain-shortened match.

Skip next section Pranavi Urs scripts history, wins Asian Games golf gold

Pranavi Urs scripts history, wins Asian Games golf gold

Pranavi Urs has become the first Indian woman to win gold in the Asian Games individual golf after she sank a nerve-wracking three-foot par putt on the final green to clinch the title by one stroke, finishing at 15-under par.

Teammates Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar celebrated by soaking Urs with water as her win was confirmed.

China's Yin Ruoning and Singapore's Shannon Tan tied for silver and bronze a stroke back, with Yin claiming silver after a playoff.

This is India's first gold in the sport since Shiv Kapur's men's title in 2002. Urs, Ashok and Dagar also came together to win India its first-ever team silver in the event. China won team gold, with Taiwan's team, featuring five-time major champion Tseng Ya-ni, taking bronze.

Skip next section CJP calls for mass Delhi march on October 10

CJP calls for mass Delhi march on October 10

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced it will mobilize a nationwide march on New Delhi next weekend unless Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns.

The call follows a protest at Mumbai's Shivaji Park that drew thousands of demonstrators despite police denying permission for the gathering.

A similar protest at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar saw several opposition politicians and student leaders being detained on Friday, which is also observed as Gandhi Jayanti to honor the birth of Mahatma Gandhi, a global pioneer of nonviolence.

"If Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign, cockroaches from across India will march to Delhi and protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10," CJP founder and convener Abhijeet Dipke said in the statement.

"And if the Delhi Police tries to stop us, wherever they stop us will become our Jantar Mantar. Ours will be a peaceful protest. We will walk on the path shown by Mahatma Gandhi."

Calling on people to join the march to preserve free and fair elections in the country, Dipke called it "a fight to save our democracy."

The announcement follows a tense October 2, when Delhi Police detained more than 700 demonstrators, including former Delhi Chief Minister Atishi, from Jantar Mantar and surrounding areas, local media reported.

Police had denied permission for the Delhi gathering and imposed Section 163 restrictions barring assemblies of more than five people.

The CJP-led gathering in Mumbai's Shivaji Park also saw a huge turnout, including film actors and musicians, but did not face a similar violent crackdown from authorities.

It is the latest flashpoint in a months-long movement that began as online satire in May and escalated into repeated street demonstrations, including a July 20 protest where Delhi Police used batons to disperse crowds. It led to the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in late July.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from India this weekend.

The Cockroach Janta Party is back for round two, calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The movement's leaders have announced that they will march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on October 10, just weeks after CJP protests led to the resignation of India's education minister.

Meanwhile, things are heating up in Japan as cricket archrivals India and Pakistan face off in the gold medal match at the Asian Games. India has posted a total of 211, setting up an uphill task for its neighbors.

For these stories and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his United List party
entries.summary: Latvia's prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.
entries.content:
Latvia

Latvia: PM's party wins biggest vote since independence

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 4, 2026

Latvia's prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.

The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.

What do the results show?

With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the left-leaning Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.

Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.

An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.

Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, was dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties proposed any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets were deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany news: Many believe Merkel more capable than Merz
entries.summary: Nearly half of Germans view former Chancellor Angela Merkel as better suited to handle Germany's challenges than current Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Also, today is the last day of Oktoberfest in Munich. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: 48% believe Merkel more capable than Merz

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 4, 2026

Nearly half of Germans view former Chancellor Angela Merkel as better suited to handle Germany's challenges than current Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Also, today is the last day of Oktoberfest in Munich. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • 48% of Germans say former Chancellor Angela Merkel is more suited to deal with Germany's challenges than current Chancellor Friedrich Merz

  • Meanwhile, Merz is visiting Kyiv as Ukraine faces a fifth winter of Russia's invasion

  • Today marks the last Germany's famous Oktoberfest event in Munich

  • On Saturday, Germany's leaders gathered in the northern city of Bremen for official festivities marking Unity Day

  • German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier warned that Germany's democracy is being challenged again, pointing to the threat from right-wing extremism

  • The national holiday commemorates October 3, 1990, when the former East Germany joined the Federal Republic of Germany

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 3, and Sunday, October 4, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Ultralight plane crash kills 2 in southwestern Germany

Ultralight plane crash kills 2 in southwestern Germany

Two people have died after a two-seater ultralight aircraft crashed into a vineyard in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

The aircraft was approaching a nearby airfield shortly after noon when it aborted its landing for unknown reasons, police said.

It then clipped a fence, collided with a tree and crashed into a vineyard near the town of Gundelsheim, where it caught fire.

Both people on board were found dead in the burned-out aircraft. Police said there were no indications that anyone else had been on board.

The victims have not yet been identified. The aircraft's origin is also unclear because its registration number was no longer legible after the fire.

Police and aviation experts are investigating whether pilot error or a technical fault caused the Sunday crash.

Skip next section Oktoberfest attended by record 7.4 million people this year

Oktoberfest attended by record 7.4 million people this year

Oktoberfest in Munich this year was attended by a record 7.4 million people, city authorities said.  

This figure exceeds the previous record of 7.2 million in 2023.

Of that 7.4 million, 447,000 went to the Olde Wiesn, which showcases what Oktoberfest looked like 100 years ago. 

Munich authorities also said 6.7 millon liters of beer was consumed during the event, which lasts more than two weeks.

Food sales also spiked 2-3% this year due to high demand for roast chicken.

However, it wasn't all fun, food and drinking during this year's Oktoberfest however.

A 47-year-old was rushed to the hospital on Sunday after suffering serious injuries at the ship swing ride in the Olde Wiesn area. It comes after a 52-year-old man was killed at the freefall tower ride on September 21.

Skip next section Germany's culture minister pays tribute to Holocaust survivor Irene Butter

Germany's culture minister pays tribute to Holocaust survivor Irene Butter

German-American Holocaust survivor Irene Butter passed away on Friday at the age of 95.

Born in 1930 to a Jewish family, the Hasenbergs, in Berlin, her family later fled persecution to Amsterdam in 1937.  

Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940 and in 1943 Butter and her family was sent to Westerbork transit camp.

In 1944, the Hasenbergs were sent to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in northern Germany. During that time Butter crossed paths with Anne Frank. 

Butter's father had arranged to get Ecuadorian travel documents for the Hasenberg family.

In 1945, Butter's family was able to leave Germany for Switzerland as part of an exchange programs for Jewish people who obtained South American passports. Butter's father, however, died on the way to Switzerland.

Butter was sent to Algeria that year, while her family stayed behind in Switzerland. Butter then immigrated to the US and her family later rejoined her in New York City.

Butter later became a public health professor at the University of Michigan. She gave talks about her experiences as a Holocaust survivor and was also a peace activist.   

"With the passing of Irene Butter, we lose an inspiring voice of remembrance and a tireless advocate for peace," German Commissioner for Culture and the Media Wolfram Weimer said on Sunday.

"Her courage to speak out and share her personal story as a Jewish woman is invaluable."

Butter received the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany in 2024.

Skip next section Welfare groups, unions urge Berlin to stop social spending cuts

Welfare groups, unions urge Berlin to stop social spending cuts

A coalition of welfare groups and unions has urged the German government not to go through with planned cuts to social spending, particularly to the elderly care system.

"Social cohesion is a prerequisite for democratic stability," the coalition of 14 bodies said.

The German Cabinet, which consists of ministers belonging to Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right CDU, the Bavarian sister party CSU, and the center-left SPD, approved a bill late last month to reform the care system. The sector has come under increasing pressure due to the aging population.  

The reform means that childless employees will pay higher surcharges for long-term care insurance and high-income earners will also have to pay more.

There will also be a reassessment of different care levels, which correspond to the benefits and services people receive. Care workers will also be burdened with additional tasks.

The reform, which aims to plug a budget gap of around €8 billion ($9 billion) in the coming year, still needs to undergo further steps in the legislative process, such as getting passed in the Bundestag.

The coalition, which includes the Verdi union and social welfare organizations such as Caritas, said it was essential that adequate care was provided alongside safe staffing levels.

The alliance said it was concerned the government was also planning cuts to other areas, including housing and youth support.

It also called for additional wealth and inheritance taxes.

Skip next section Germany's environment minister calls for water policy overhaul

Germany's environment minister calls for water policy overhaul

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany needs to formulate a new approach to water policy after a summer of heat waves and low river levels.

"The days when we in Germany didn't have to worry about water are definitely over. Germany needs a different approach to water," Schneider told the Cologne-based Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper.

The minister cited low water levels on the Rhine River in western Germany and Lake Constance in the south as a problem for both the natural environment and the economy. 

Schneider is expected to take part in a meeting on Monday in Berlin along with EU Environment Commissoner Jessika Roswall and representatives from the public, private and non-profit sectors. At the meeting, they will discuss what a new approach to water policy will look like.

The minister said technical water infrastructure must be upgraded to retain water in the landscape.

"If the mountains and their glaciers fail to supply water, rivers, floodplains, forest and soils must serve as water reservoirs," Schneider said.

The German government has provided €100 billion ($114 billion) to state and municipal authorities as part of a special fund to upgrade water infrastructure.

Skip next section Deutsche Bahn to offer 'Family Ticket' permanently

Deutsche Bahn to offer 'Family Ticket' permanently

Germany's rail operator Deutsche Bahn intends to offer its "Family Ticket" (Familienticket) deal permanently from November. 

The "Family Ticket" is a €99.99 roundtrip to and from a destination for two adults and several kids up to a total of five people. The "Family Ticket" includes seat reservations on the high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train.

The deal was first offered this summer and led to a significant rise in Deutsche Bahn ridership.

"We were able to welcome 100,000 more families on board our trains than last year," Deutsche Bahn CEO Evelyn Palla told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

The "Family Ticket" will be available for purchase starting on October 26.

Although families may be able to get a nice deal on a ticket, they may also still have to reckon with delays and cancellations that have plagued Deutsche Bahn in recent years.

"A large part of our infrastructure is too old, too prone to malfunctions, and breaks down too often," Palla said. "We can only renew the system bit by bit and cannot make up in one or two years what has been neglected for many years:"

The Deutsche Bahn CEO said said renovations on the rail network will take at least 10 years and improvements will only be noticed by passengers once a large part of the rail equipment has been replaced.

Skip next section Munich's Oktoberfest beer festival draws to a close

Munich's Oktoberfest beer festival draws to a close

Germany's famous Oktoberfest in Munich is holding its last day of celebrations on Sunday.

At noon (1000 GMT), marksmen are expected to perform a gun salute at the foot of the Bavaria statue to mark the symbolic end to the festival.

We will also hear figures later on the number of visitors to this year's event, which began on September 19, and the amount of beer consumed.

Skip next section Merz in Kyiv as Ukraine faces fifth winter amid Russian invasion

Merz in Kyiv as Ukraine faces fifth winter amid Russian invasion

German Chancellor Merz is in Kyiv on an unannounced visit, along with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and other leading German economic figures.

Merz is expected to announce new military aid for Ukraine along with other initatives as Ukraine faces its fifth winter amid Russia's ongoing invasion.

Skip next section Nearly half of Germans think Merkel better suited than Merz to tackle Germany's challenges

Nearly half of Germans think Merkel better suited than Merz to tackle Germany's challenges

A new survey from YouGov which was commissioned by German news agency DPA found that 48% of Germans believe former Chancellor Angela Merkel is better suited to tackle Germany's challenges than current Chancellor Friedrich Merz. 

The poll also found that 29% of Germans believe the two leaders would be equally capable of confronting Germany's problems.

Only 8% viewed Merkel less favorably than Merz; 15% didn't answer the survey or said they didn't know how to respond.

Both Merkel and Merz are members of the center-right Christian Democratic Union, but have long been political rivals.

Merkel served as chancellor for a period of 16 years from 2005 to 2021.

Merz, meanwhile, faces record low approval ratings since becoming chancellor in May last year.

Germany's problems include a stagnant economy, rising energy prices, an aging population with fewer working to support social programs, illegal immigration and foreign policy challenges such as the Russian invasion of Ukraine, among other issues.

Skip next section Welcome back!

Welcome back!

Welcome back to our coverage this Sunday on what's happening in Germany.

Nearly half of Germans feel that former German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who governed for 16 years, is better suited than incumbent Chancellor Friedrich Merz to tackle the country's current problems, according to a new survey. 

Both Merz and Merkel belong to the conservative Christian Democratic Union party.

The poll results come as Merz faces record low approval ratings as chancellor since he took the reigns in May last year.

Also on Sunday, the chancellor paid an unannounced visit to Kyiv to show solidarity with Ukraine amid Russia's ongoing invasion.

And it's closing time! One last call for alcohol ― today's the last day of Oktoberfest in Munich.  

All this and more from the heart of Europe. Stay tuned throughout the day.

Skip next section That's it for today

That's it for today

German Unity Day's official celebrations have ended, and we're pausing our coverage.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making news in Germany.

Skip next section Thousands attend anti-war demonstrations in Berlin, Stuttgart

Thousands attend anti-war demonstrations in Berlin, Stuttgart

Thousands of people protested against war, military buildup and possible conscription in Berlin and Stuttgart on Saturday.

Among other things, the protesters called for a end to all economic sanctions and arms shipments, calling instead for increased social spending.

Protesters in Berlin marched from the Brandenburg Gate through the city center. Police estimated there were 5,800 attendees while organizers put the turnout at 20,000 people.

The organizers in Stuttgart estimated a turnout of around 15,000 people. However, dpa journalists who were present at the demonstration estimated the turnout to be in the low to mid thousands.

Skip next section After Bremen, Düsseldorf next up to host German Unity Day

After Bremen, Düsseldorf next up to host German Unity Day

Düsseldorf has been announced as the host city for next year's official commemoration of German Unity Day.

The annual event is hosted by whichever state holds the rotating presidency of the upper house of Germany's parliament, known as the Bundesrat. In 2027, it will be held by Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia.

Düsseldorf is the second-largest city in North-Rhine Westphalia, after Cologne. The state is also home to the industrial cities of the Ruhr Valley including Dortmund, Essen, Duisburg and Bochum.

The mayor of Bremen, Andreas Bovenschulte, symbolically handed the baton to North Rhine-Westphalia's premier Hendrik Wüst, who will take up his post as president of the Bundesrat on January 1.

"Togetherness, connection, and unity are never a finished task," said Wüst.

"Continuing to work on this, maintaining one's interest, and keeping the conversation going — even with people whose outlook might be completely different from one's own," he added.

Skip next section East German economy still trails west 36 years after reunification

East German economy still trails west 36 years after reunification

More than three decades after German reunification, the economy in the eastern states still lags beind the western states.

The five eastern German states reached just under 79% of western Germany's economic level in 2025, according to an analysis by the German Economic Institute (IW) released on German Unity Day.

The figure is based on an index designed to track eastern Germany's economic convergence with the west. It incorporates economic output per capita, productivity, investment, research and development, employment, unemployment and self-employment.

Although the east has made substantial progress since 1991, when the index stood at 51% of the west's economic development, this convergence has stalled over the past five years, hovering between between 78% and 79%.

The researchers pointed to large shortcomings in research and development (R&D) in particular. They found that the number of research and development personnel in the east was equivalent to just over 46% of the same workforce in the west.

The researchers also noted that demographic change could affect economic convergence between the east and the west.

Without immigration, eastern Germany's population will shrink by more than a fifth by 2045. This would make it particularly dependent on skilled migration.

But the German Economic Institute noted that support for the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party (AfD) in recent state elections has called into question the region's openness to migration.

Skip next section Oktoberfest crowds surge toward 7 million mark

Oktoberfest crowds surge toward 7 million mark

Munich's Oktoberfest is on course for one of its busiest years, with 5.2 million visitors recorded through Wednesday.

That was around 700,000 more than at the same point last year, according to anonymized mobile phone data analyzed for the dpa news agency.

If the strong attendance continues through the final weekend, visitor numbers could approach 7 million. The record stands at 7.2 million in 2023, although that year's Oktoberfest ran for two days longer.

Good weather is thought to have helped boost attendance this year.

International visitors now account for around 31% of the crowd, six percentage points more than two years ago. Americans are the largest group of foreign visitors, followed by Italians.

Around 58,000 Italians attended during the middle weekend alone, traditionally known in Munich as "Italian weekend."

Visitors are also getting older. The average age this year is 46, with people aged 50 to 59 making up the largest group at around 23%. The share of 18- to 29-year-olds has fallen by 5.1 percentage points compared with two years ago to 21.5%.

Visitors spend an average of just over five and a half hours at the festival.

entries.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
entries.summary: Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia government forces reclaim Tigray capital airport

October 4, 2026

Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.

Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.

Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.

"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.

The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.

Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.

Return to civil war?

Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.

The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.

The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.

The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.

Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.

The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.

Fears of wider regional unrest

The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.

For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.

Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.

The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.

Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea

The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
